title: Balancing, Filtering & Decoupling
description: Reject common-mode noise by balance, design filters for the impedances they sit between, and decouple analog and digital supplies and the mains.

study.title: Balanced circuits and CMRR
study.body: A circuit is **balanced** when both signal conductors, and everything connected to them, have the same impedance to ground. Noise then couples equally into both wires: it is **common mode** and cancels in a differential load. Any imbalance converts part of $V_{cm}$ into a differential voltage $V_{dm}$; with a source imbalance $\Delta R_s$ and a balanced load $R_L$ per side (signal source not drawn), $\mathrm{CMRR} \approx 20\log(R_L/\Delta R_s)$. Balancing and shielding are independent, so their dB values add.

study.title: Differential and instrumentation amplifiers
study.body: A unity-gain difference amplifier made of four resistors with tolerance $p$ has a worst-case CMRR of about $20\log(1/2p)$: 54 dB with 0.1 % resistors. Its common-mode input resistance is only about $R_1 + R_2$ per input, so an unbalanced source $R_s$ limits the CMRR to about $20\log\frac{R_1+R_2}{R_s}$, ≈ $20\log(R_2/R_s)$ for a high-gain stage ($R_2 \gg R_1$). An **instrumentation amplifier** puts all the gain in two high-impedance buffers **before** the unity-gain difference stage, so the CMRR improves by the gain. Ground a long input cable's shield at the source end: grounded at the amplifier, the cable capacitance shunts the high common-mode input impedance (a trade-off, since emissions favour grounding both ends).

study.title: Filters need an impedance mismatch
study.body: A **series** element only attenuates if its impedance is large compared with $Z_S + Z_L$; a **shunt** element only if it is small compared with $Z_S \parallel Z_L$. Low source and high load impedance (typical for common-mode noise: PCB ground → cable antenna) needs an L-filter: series ferrite or inductor facing the low side, capacitor to chassis facing the high side. With a series $Z$ and a shunt $C$ in each line, common mode sees $Z/2$ and $2C$, the differential signal $2Z$ and $C/2$; so the series part is made a **common-mode choke**. Parasitics turn every low-pass filter into a high-pass above some frequency: layout matters.

study.title: Explore: damping an LC supply filter
study.body: An RC decoupling filter costs supply voltage; an LC filter attenuates more (40 dB/decade above $f_r$) with hardly any DC drop, but it **resonates** and can amplify noise near $f_r$. The peak is set by the damping $\zeta = \frac{R}{2}\sqrt{C/L}$, with $R$ the total series resistance; keep $\zeta \geq 0.5$ (peak ≈ 1.2 dB). Here $L$ = 10 µH and $C$ = 10 µF ($f_r$ ≈ 15.9 kHz): drag $R$ (grey: an RC filter with the same corner). From a noise point of view a dissipative (RC) filter is preferred: it turns noise into heat instead of moving it into an inductor's field.

study.title: Decoupling digital ICs
study.body: Switching CMOS outputs charge their loads: $I = nC_LV_{CC}/t_r$, a roughly triangular pulse $2t_r$ wide. A local capacitor supplies this charge while the rail may drop at most $\Delta V$. But a decoupling capacitor is a series **LC network**: its ESL (0.5–2 nH for SMD) plus pads, traces and vias (a PCB trace roughly 0.4–0.6 nH per mm, a through via about 0.8 nH) and the IC package. Above $f_r$ the network is inductive and its capacitance value no longer matters: only less inductance helps.

study.title: Explore: many capacitors and antiresonance
study.body: $n$ identical capacitors, spread out so their loops do not couple, give $nC$ and $L/n$: lower impedance at all high frequencies. Mixing values adds a dip but also a **parallel resonance** (antiresonance) between the dips, where the large capacitor is already inductive and the small one still capacitive. Drag $C_2$ (each branch 2 nH, 20 mΩ). Design for a **target impedance** $Z_t = k\,\Delta V/\Delta I$ up to the knee $1/(\pi t_r)$, which needs $n \geq 2L/(Z_t t_r)$. Ott takes $k$ = 2, since only about half of the transient current lies below the knee ($k$ = 1 is the strict choice). Bulk capacitors (5–100 µF, more than the sum of the local ones) cover the low frequencies.

study.title: Power-line filters
study.body: A mains filter has a **common-mode** section, a choke $L_{CM}$ (typically 2–10 mH) with **Y capacitors** from each line to the chassis, and a **differential-mode** section, the **X capacitor** across the lines with the choke's leakage inductance. The Y capacitors leak current to protective earth, $I = 2\pi fC_YV$, which safety standards limit (0.5 mA to a few mA), so they stay at a few nF. Conducted emissions are measured with a **LISN**, which gives each line a defined 50 Ω. Mount the filter where the cord enters, with its case bonded directly to the chassis.

steps.title: Balanced circuits
steps.body: In a **balanced** circuit both conductors, and the source and load connected to them, have the same impedance to ground. Noise picked up by the pair is then the same on both wires (**common mode**), and a differential load ignores it. A circuit with a grounded return conductor is unbalanced (single-ended).

steps.prompt: A source has 100 Ω in series with each output terminal and drives a load with 10 kΩ from each input to ground. One of the two source voltages is zero. This circuit is balanced.
steps.explanation: Balance is about the **impedances** to ground, not the signal voltages. Both conductors see 100 Ω + 10 kΩ, so noise couples equally into both. One (or even both) of the source voltages may be zero and the circuit is still balanced.

steps.title: Common-mode rejection ratio
steps.body: No circuit is perfectly balanced, so a common-mode voltage $V_{cm}$ produces a small differential voltage $V_{dm}$ across the load. The CMRR says how much smaller it is. 40–80 dB is a realistic value for a well-designed circuit; more requires trimming and special cables.

steps.prompt: A ground-potential difference puts {{Vcm|V}} of common-mode voltage on a balanced pair. The load sees {{Vdm|V}} of differential noise. What is the CMRR?
steps.explanation: $\mathrm{CMRR} = 20\log(V_{cm}/V_{dm})$ = 20 log({{Vcm|V}} / {{Vdm|V}}) = 20 log({{Vcm/Vdm||3}}) = {{20*log10(Vcm/Vdm)|dB}}.

steps.title: Source unbalance
steps.body: Often the load is balanced but the source is not. The common-mode voltage drives current through both legs; the difference $\Delta R_s$ between the source resistances turns it into a differential voltage. For $R_L \gg R_s$ the CMRR depends only on the ratio below. A single-ended source (one side grounded) has $\Delta R_s = R_s$. Improve it by reducing the imbalance or by raising the common-mode load resistance.

steps.prompt: A single-ended sensor with {{dRs|Ω}} output resistance feeds a balanced input with {{RL|Ω}} from each input to ground. Estimate the CMRR.
steps.explanation: One side of the source is grounded, so the whole source resistance is the imbalance: $\Delta R_s$ = {{dRs|Ω}}. $\mathrm{CMRR} \approx 20\log(R_L/\Delta R_s)$ = 20 log({{RL|Ω}} / {{dRs|Ω}}) = {{20*log10(RL/dRs)|dB}}.

steps.title: Filters work by mismatch
steps.body: A filter attenuates by putting an impedance mismatch in the noise path. A **series** element only helps if its impedance is large compared with $Z_S + Z_L$; a **shunt** element only if it is small compared with $Z_S \parallel Z_L$. So: low source and load impedance → series element; both high → shunt capacitor; one low and one high → no single element works, use an L-filter with the series part facing the low impedance.

steps.prompt: Common-mode noise comes from the PCB ground (low impedance) and drives a cable that acts as an antenna (high impedance). Which filter at the I/O connector works best?
options: Ferrite on the board side, capacitor to chassis on the cable side
Capacitor to chassis on the board side, ferrite on the cable side
steps.explanation: Source low, load high: no single element works, since a ferrite would have to beat the high cable impedance and a capacitor the low ground impedance. In an L-filter the ferrite faces the low-impedance side and raises the source impedance, so the capacitor on the high-impedance cable side can shunt the noise to chassis. Reversed, the capacitor fights the low ground impedance and the ferrite only adds to an already high load.

steps.prompt: Each line of a two-wire cable gets a series impedance $Z$ and a shunt capacitor $C$ to chassis. Match what each mode sees.
steps.explanation: Common mode drives both lines together, so the two branches are in **parallel**: $Z/2$ and $2C$. A differential signal goes out on one line and back on the other, so the elements are in **series**: $2Z$ and $C/2$. The capacitors favour common-mode filtering, but plain series impedance would hit the signal harder than the noise. That is why the series part is built as a common-mode choke, which has almost no differential impedance.

steps.prompt: A π-filter (ferrite bead between two capacitors) that gives 40 dB at 10 MHz will give at least 40 dB at 1 GHz too.
steps.explanation: Parasitics take over at high frequency: the capacitance across the ferrite bypasses it, and the inductance of the capacitor leads, pads and vias makes the shunt elements inductive. Above some frequency the low-pass becomes a high-pass filter. With a poor layout this happens at tens of MHz; a good layout pushes it to hundreds of MHz.

steps.prompt: A balanced input with a CMRR of {{CM}} dB sees {{Vcm|V}} of common-mode noise. How large is the differential noise at the load?
A source with {{Rs|Ω}} in each leg feeds a balanced load made of two {{RL|Ω}} resistors with {{pp}} % tolerance. What is the worst-case CMRR?
steps.explanation: Worst case one load resistor is $p$ high and the other $p$ low, so $\Delta R_L/R_L = 2p$ = {{2*p}}. $\mathrm{CMRR} \approx 20\log\left(\frac{1}{2p}\cdot\frac{R_L}{R_s}\right)$ = 20 log({{1/(2*p)||3}} × {{RL/Rs||3}}) = {{20*log10(RL/(2*p*Rs))|dB}}. A low source and a high load resistance help as much as tight tolerances.

steps.prompt: An unshielded balanced pair picks up {{Vp|V}} of common-mode noise from an electric field. A shield with {{SE}} dB shielding effectiveness is added, and the circuit has {{CM}} dB of balance (CMRR). What differential noise reaches the load?
steps.explanation: The shield reduces the common-mode pickup, and the balance then converts only a fraction of what remains into differential noise, so the dB values add: {{SE}} + {{CM}} = {{SE+CM}} dB. $V_{dm}$ = {{Vp|V}} × $10^{-{{(SE+CM)/20}}}$ = {{Vp*10^(-(SE+CM)/20)|V}}.

steps.prompt: The common-mode rejection is limited by resistors with {{pp}} % tolerance (worst case).

ask.prompt: Find the CMRR of a unity-gain difference amplifier built with these resistors.
ask.explanation: Resistor mismatch converts common mode into a differential error: $\mathrm{CMRR} \approx 20\log\frac{1}{2p}$ = 20 log({{1/(2*p)||3}}) = {{20*log10(1/(2*p))|dB}}.

ask.prompt: Find the CMRR of an instrumentation amplifier with gain {{G}}, all of it in the input buffers.
ask.explanation: The buffers amplify the differential signal by $A_{dm}$ = {{G}} but pass common mode with gain 1. Only then does the unity-gain difference stage convert part of the common mode: $\mathrm{CMRR} \approx 20\log\frac{A_{dm}}{2p}$ = 20 log {{G}} + 20 log({{1/(2*p)||3}}) = {{20*log10(G)|dB}} + {{20*log10(1/(2*p))|dB}} = {{20*log10(G/(2*p))|dB}}: the gain in the buffers adds directly to the CMRR.

steps.prompt: A single-ended source with {{Rs|Ω}} output resistance drives a high-impedance differential amplifier through {{len}} m of shielded cable ({{Cpm|F}} per metre). The shield is grounded at the amplifier, so the cable capacitance shunts the common-mode input. Estimate the best possible CMRR at {{f|Hz}}.
steps.explanation: The common-mode load can be no higher than the cable reactance. $C$ = {{len}} m × {{Cpm|F}}/m = {{C|F}}, $X_C = 1/(2\pi fC)$ = {{X|Ω}}. With $\Delta R_s = R_s$: $\mathrm{CMRR} \approx 20\log(X_C/\Delta R_s)$ = 20 log({{X|Ω}} / {{Rs|Ω}}) = {{20*log10(X/Rs)|dB}}. Grounding the shield at the **source** end puts this capacitance across the low source resistance instead.

steps.prompt: A {{C|F}} capacitor is placed across the line between a {{Rs|Ω}} source and a {{RL|Ω}} load (both resistive). What insertion loss does it give at {{f|Hz}}?
steps.explanation: The capacitor works against the Thévenin resistance seen from the load, $R_S \parallel R_L$ = {{Rp|Ω}}. It divides the load voltage by $|1 + j\omega C(R_S\parallel R_L)|$: $\omega C R_p$ = {{k||3}}, so IL = $20\log\sqrt{1 + (\omega CR_p)^2}$ = {{10*log10(1+k^2)|dB}}. A shunt capacitor needs a high-impedance environment.

steps.prompt: A ferrite bead that is essentially resistive, {{Zf|Ω}} at the noise frequency, is placed in series between a {{Rs|Ω}} source and a {{RL|Ω}} load. What insertion loss does it give?
steps.explanation: Without the bead the load gets $V\frac{R_L}{R_S+R_L}$, with it $V\frac{R_L}{R_S+R_L+Z_f}$. IL = $20\log\frac{R_S + R_L + Z_f}{R_S + R_L}$ = 20 log({{Rs+RL+Zf|Ω}} / {{Rs+RL|Ω}}) = {{20*log10((Rs+RL+Zf)/(Rs+RL))|dB}}. A series element only works when $Z_f \gg R_S + R_L$: ferrites belong in low-impedance circuits.

steps.prompt: An LC filter feeds a sensitive analog stage: $L$ = {{L|H}} with {{R|Ω}} winding resistance and $C$ = {{C|F}}.

ask.prompt: Find the resonant frequency of the filter.
ask.explanation: $f_r = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$ = 1 / (2π √({{L|H}} × {{C|F}})) = {{1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C))|Hz}}. Keep this well below the frequencies at which the circuit has gain or the noise is.
$\zeta = \frac{R}{2}\sqrt{C/L}$ = {{R/2}} × √({{C|F}} / {{L|H}}) = {{z||3}}. Well below 0.5: the filter peaks by about {{20*log10(1/(2*z*sqrt(1 - z^2)))|dB}} at resonance.

ask.prompt: What total series resistance would give $\zeta$ = 0.5?
ask.explanation: $\zeta = \frac{R}{2}\sqrt{C/L}$ = 0.5 gives $R = \sqrt{L/C}$ = √({{L|H}} / {{C|F}}) = {{sqrt(L/C)|Ω}}, so add about {{sqrt(L/C) - R|Ω}} in series (or a damping resistor elsewhere).

steps.prompt: The LC supply filter ($L$ = 10 µH, $C$ = 10 µF) peaks at resonance. Set the series resistance $R$ so the resonance peak is {{Pk}} dB.
steps.explanation: The peak gain is $\frac{1}{2\zeta\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}$ = {{M||3}} ({{Pk}} dB) for $\zeta$ = {{zt||3}}. Here $\sqrt{C/L}$ = 1 Ω⁻¹, so $\zeta = R/2$ and $R$ = {{Rt|Ω}}. More resistance damps the peak further but costs DC voltage drop.

steps.title: Supplying the switching current
steps.body: Each low-to-high output transition charges the load capacitance (a CMOS input is typically 7–12 pF). The current pulse is roughly triangular, $2t_r$ wide. The decoupling capacitor next to the IC must supply it while the rail drops less than $\Delta V$.

steps.prompt: An IC switches {{n}} outputs at the same moment, each driving {{CL|F}} of load capacitance, from a {{Vcc|V}} supply with a rise time of {{tr|s}}. Estimate the transient supply current.
steps.explanation: $I = \frac{nC_LV_{CC}}{t_r}$ = {{n}} × {{CL|F}} × {{Vcc|V}} / {{tr|s}} = {{n*CL*Vcc/tr|A}}.

steps.prompt: A current step of {{dI|A}} lasting {{dt|s}} may not pull the {{Vcc|V}} rail down by more than {{pct}} %. What is the minimum decoupling capacitance?
steps.explanation: $\Delta V$ = {{pct}} % × {{Vcc|V}} = {{dV|V}}. $C \geq \frac{\Delta I\,\Delta t}{\Delta V}$ = {{dI|A}} × {{dt|s}} / {{dV|V}} = {{dI*dt/dV|F}}.

steps.prompt: A {{C|F}} capacitor (ESL {{ESL|H}}) connects to the IC through {{lt}} mm of trace in total (≈ 0.6 nH/mm) and {{nv}} vias (≈ 0.8 nH each). Find the resonant frequency of this decoupling network.
steps.explanation: Total series inductance: $L$ = {{ESL|H}} + {{lt}} × 0.6 nH + {{nv}} × 0.8 nH = {{Lt|H}}. $f_r = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$ = 1 / (2π √({{Lt|H}} × {{C|F}})) = {{1/(2*pi*sqrt(Lt*C))|Hz}}. Note how the mounting, not the capacitor, dominates the inductance.

steps.prompt: At 1 GHz, replacing a 100 nF decoupling capacitor by a 1 nF one in the same package, on the same pads, lowers the decoupling impedance considerably.
steps.explanation: With about 1.5 nH of mounted inductance the 100 nF network resonates near 13 MHz and the 1 nF one near 130 MHz. At 1 GHz both are far above resonance and look like the same inductance: $2\pi fL$ ≈ 9.4 Ω, while $1/(2\pi fC)$ is only 0.16 Ω for 1 nF. Only less inductance helps there (smaller package, more vias, more capacitors in parallel); the smaller value only worsens the low-frequency decoupling.

steps.prompt: An IC on a {{Vcc|V}} rail draws transient current steps of {{dI|A}}; the rail may vary by {{dVp}} %. Each mounted decoupling capacitor has {{L|H}} of total inductance, and the edges take {{tr|s}}. Use Ott's target impedance $Z_t = k\,\Delta V/\Delta I$ with $k$ = 2.

ask.prompt: Find the target impedance of the power distribution network.
ask.explanation: $\Delta V$ = {{dVp}} % × {{Vcc|V}} = {{dV|V}}. $Z_t = 2\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}$ = 2 × {{dV|V}} / {{dI|A}} = {{Zt|Ω}}. The factor 2 allows for only about half of the transient current lying below $1/(\pi t_r)$.

ask.prompt: How many capacitors are needed so their combined inductance stays below the target impedance up to $1/(\pi t_r)$? Round up.
ask.explanation: $Z_t = 2\Delta V/\Delta I$ = {{Zt|Ω}}. At $f = 1/(\pi t_r)$ = {{1/(pi*tr)|Hz}}, $n$ capacitors in parallel have $2\pi fL/n = \frac{2L}{nt_r}$. Requiring this ≤ $Z_t$: $n \geq \frac{2L}{Z_t t_r}$ = 2 × {{L|H}} / ({{Zt|Ω}} × {{tr|s}}) = {{nn||3}}, so {{ceil(nn)}} capacitors.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the impedance of a 100 nF and a 1 nF capacitor in parallel, each with 2 nH of mounting inductance. What causes the peak between the two dips?
options: A parallel resonance: the 100 nF branch is already inductive while the 1 nF branch is still capacitive
The series resonance of the 1 nF capacitor with its inductance
The series resonance of the 100 nF capacitor with its inductance
The ESR of the 100 nF capacitor
steps.explanation: The dips are the series resonances: 100 nF with 2 nH at 11 MHz, 1 nF with 2 nH at 113 MHz. In between, the 100 nF branch behaves as an inductor and the 1 nF branch as a capacitor; together they form a parallel LC circuit with a high impedance peak (antiresonance), here near 80 MHz. Equal-value capacitors avoid this.

steps.title: Mains filters
steps.body: A power-line filter has a **common-mode** section, the choke $L_{CM}$ plus **Y capacitors** from each line to chassis, and a **differential-mode** section, the **X capacitor** across the lines with the choke's leakage inductance. The Y capacitors leak mains current into the protective earth; safety rules cap that current (0.5 mA to a few mA), so they are only a few nF. Emission tests use a **LISN** to give each line a defined 50 Ω and keep mains noise out of the measurement.

steps.prompt: A filter on a {{V}} V, {{f}} Hz mains supply has Y capacitors from line and from neutral to the protective earth.

ask.prompt: How much leakage current flows through a {{CY|F}} Y capacitor connected to the line conductor?
ask.explanation: $I = 2\pi fC_YV$ = 2π × {{f}} Hz × {{CY|F}} × {{V}} V = {{2*pi*f*CY*V|A}}. (The capacitor on the neutral has almost no voltage across it.)

ask.prompt: The filter may use at most half of a {{Ilim|A}} leakage limit. What is the largest allowed Y capacitor?
ask.explanation: Half the limit is {{Ilim/2|A}}. $C_Y \leq \frac{I}{2\pi fV}$ = {{Ilim/2|A}} / (2π × {{f}} Hz × {{V}} V) = {{Ilim/2/(2*pi*f*V)|F}}.

steps.prompt: Match each part of a mains filter to its role.
steps.explanation: The common-mode choke's windings cancel each other's flux for the mains current, so it only impedes common-mode noise; the Y capacitors shunt that noise to chassis. Imperfect coupling leaves a small leakage inductance in series with each line, which together with the X capacitor forms the differential-mode filter.

steps.prompt: A clock buffer switches {{n}} loads of {{CL|F}} at once from {{Vcc|V}} with {{tr|s}} edges. Its rail may dip at most {{dV|V}}. Treating the current pulse as a triangle of height $I$ and width $2t_r$, find the minimum decoupling capacitance.
steps.explanation: Peak current $I = nC_LV_{CC}/t_r$ = {{n*CL*Vcc/tr|A}}. The triangle's charge is $\frac{1}{2}I \cdot 2t_r = It_r$ = {{n*CL*Vcc|C}}, exactly the charge $nC_LV_{CC}$ that the loads take. $C \geq Q/\Delta V$ = {{n*CL*Vcc|C}} / {{dV|V}} = {{n*CL*Vcc/dV|F}}, independent of the rise time.

steps.prompt: A processor on a {{Vcc|V}} rail draws {{dI|A}} transients with {{tr|s}} edges; the rail may vary {{pct}} %. Each decoupling capacitor has {{L|H}} of mounted inductance, and decoupling must work down to {{fl|Hz}} (below that the regulator takes over). Use Ott's target impedance $Z_t = 2\Delta V/\Delta I$.

ask.prompt: How many equal capacitors are needed? Round up.

ask.explanation: $Z_t = 2\Delta V/\Delta I$ = {{Zt|Ω}}. At the lowest frequency the capacitance itself must stay below $Z_t$: $\frac{1}{2\pi f C} \leq Z_t$ → $C \geq \frac{1}{2\pi f Z_t}$ = 1 / (2π × {{fl|Hz}} × {{Zt|Ω}}) = {{Ct|F}}.

ask.prompt: What minimum value should each (equal) capacitor have?
ask.explanation: $Z_t$ = {{Zt|Ω}}. Number: $n \geq 2L/(Z_tt_r)$ = {{nn||3}} → {{N}}. Total: $C \geq 1/(2\pi f Z_t)$ = {{Ct|F}}. Each capacitor: {{Ct|F}} / {{N}} = {{Ct/N|F}}; pick the next standard value in the smallest practical package.

steps.prompt: {{n}} equal decoupling capacitors of {{C|F}}, each with {{L|H}} of mounted inductance, are spread around a large IC. Estimate the magnitude of their combined impedance at {{f|Hz}} (neglect ESR and mutual coupling).
steps.explanation: One branch: $X = 2\pi fL - \frac{1}{2\pi fC}$ = {{2*pi*f*L|Ω}} − {{1/(2*pi*f*C)|Ω}} = {{X|Ω}} (inductive). $n$ equal branches in parallel divide it by $n$: |Z| = {{abs(X)|Ω}} / {{n}} = {{abs(X)/n|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: Design the common-mode section of a mains filter for {{V}} V, {{f}} Hz. The leakage limit is {{Ilim|A}}, of which the filter may use half. The common-mode corner frequency must be {{fc|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: Find the largest Y capacitor value.

ask.explanation: $C_Y = \frac{I/2}{2\pi fV}$ = {{CY|F}}. Common mode sees both Y capacitors in parallel: $2C_Y$ = {{2*CY|F}}. From $f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L\cdot 2C_Y}}$: $L = \frac{1}{(2\pi f_c)^2\,2C_Y}$ = {{Lc|H}}.

steps.prompt: A difference amplifier ($R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}}, $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}, gain $R_2/R_1$ = {{G}}) is driven by a single-ended source with {{Rs|Ω}} output resistance. A ground-potential difference of {{Vcm|V}} appears as common-mode voltage.

ask.prompt: Estimate the CMRR set by the source unbalance.
ask.explanation: The common-mode input resistance is $R_1 + R_2$ = {{Rc|Ω}} per input, and the imbalance is $R_s$: $\mathrm{CMRR} \approx 20\log\frac{R_1 + R_2}{R_s}$ = 20 log({{Rc|Ω}} / {{Rs|Ω}}) = {{CM|dB}}. Since $R_2 \gg R_1$, Ott's $20\log(R_2/R_s)$ = {{20*log10(R2/Rs)|dB}} is almost the same.

ask.prompt: Estimate the resulting noise voltage at the amplifier output.
ask.explanation: $\mathrm{CMRR} \approx 20\log\frac{R_1 + R_2}{R_s}$ = {{CM|dB}}, so the differential input error is $V_{cm}R_s/(R_1 + R_2)$ = {{Vcm*Rs/Rc|V}}. The amplifier multiplies it by its gain: {{G}} × {{Vcm*Rs/Rc|V}} = {{G*Vcm*Rs/Rc|V}}. A buffered (instrumentation) input with megohms of common-mode resistance would cut this by orders of magnitude.

steps.prompt: An op-amp stage drives 100 m of shielded cable (about 10 nF) and oscillates. Which change is the standard fix?
options: Isolate the cable with a small series resistor at the output, with a small capacitor from the output to the inverting input
Put a larger capacitor across the far end of the cable
Increase the feedback resistor so the loop gain rises
Ground the cable shield at both ends
steps.explanation: The op amp's output resistance $R_o$ and the load capacitance form a pole at $1/(2\pi R_oC_L)$ inside the feedback loop; its extra phase lag can make the feedback positive where the loop gain is still above 1. A series resistor (≈ $R_o$) isolates the load, and a 10–100 pF feedback capacitor adds a compensating phase lead. More capacitance makes it worse.

steps.prompt: Switching ripple at {{fn|Hz}} must be attenuated by {{A}} dB with an LC filter that uses $C$ = {{C|F}}. Well above resonance the filter rolls off at 40 dB/decade.

ask.prompt: What resonant frequency should the filter have?

ask.explanation: $f_r = f/10^{A/40}$ = {{fr|Hz}}. $L = \frac{1}{(2\pi f_r)^2C}$ = 1 / ((2π × {{fr|Hz}})² × {{C|F}}) = {{L|H}}. Then check the damping ($\zeta \geq 0.5$) so the filter does not amplify noise near {{fr|Hz}}.

steps.prompt: An amplifier for a 1 kHz sensor signal picks up the same noise whether its bandwidth is 10 kHz or 10 MHz, because the noise sources around it are the same.
steps.explanation: Bandwidth is an open window: everything inside it gets in, both external interference (radio, switching noise) and the circuit's own wideband noise. Use no more bandwidth than the signal needs; the same goes for logic: slower edges generate and pick up less high-frequency noise.
